children.text: Cosmic inflation

Model a homogeneous isotropic universe by an expanding uniform-density sphere of radius R(t)=a(t)Rs. Its mass-equivalent energy density is ρ, so total energy density is ρc². The first Friedmann equation is \(H^2=A_1\rho-kc^2/(R_s^2a^2)\), where H=ȧ/a and k is +1,0,−1 for closed, flat and open geometry. Adiabatic evolution has \(\dot\rho+A_2(\rho+p/c^2)H=0\), with p=wρc². Present values have subscript 0 and a0=1. Define critical mass density consistently with the first equation as ρc=H²/A1 and Ω=ρ/ρc. The source prints an extra c² in one definition of critical density, while its worked solution uses this dimensionally consistent definition. During scalar-field inflation, \(\ddot\phi+3H\dot\phi=-V^{\prime}\), \(H^2=(\dot\phi^2/2+V)/(3M_{pl}^2)\). Slow roll neglects φ̈ and kinetic energy. Define \(\epsilon=-\dot H/H^2\), \(\delta=-\ddot\phi/(H\dot\phi)\), ηV=δ+ε and dN=dln a=Hdt, with N=0 at the end. Thus N is negative before the end. Part D retains the source's requested numerical N=60 and discusses this sign convention explicitly.

children.text: a.1. First Friedmann coefficient
Use Newtonian gravity for a boundary test mass to determine A1.
a.2. Adiabatic continuity
Use the first law to determine A2.
a.3. Equations of state
Find w for radiation, nonrelativistic matter and constant energy density.
a.4. Flat-universe scale factors
For k=0 find a(t) in the three cases. Use a(0)=0 for radiation and matter, and a(t0)=1 for constant density.
a.5. Curvature-density relation
Express k through Ω,H,a,Rs and c.
a.6. Geometry ranges
Give the density-ratio range for each k.
b.1. Flatness problem
Find the time dependence of Ω−1 in radiation- and matter-dominated nearly flat universes.
b.2. Inflationary flattening
For a constant-density era and |Ω−1|≪1, find Ω−1 as a function of time.
b.3. Equivalent inflation conditions
Show that constant-density domination produces negative pressure, accelerated expansion and a decreasing comoving Hubble radius.
b.4. Slow-roll inflation bound
Show that decreasing (aH)⁻¹ means ε<1.
c.1. Potential slow-roll formulas
Estimate ε,ηV and dN/dφ using V,V′,V″.
d.1. End of monomial inflation
For V=Λ⁴(φ/Mpl)ⁿ with integer n and positive field, find φend when ε=1.
d.2. Observable constraints and e-fold sign
Using r=16ε and ns=1+2ηV−6ε at the start, express r and ns in N,n. Compare integer n to ns=0.968±0.006 and r<0.12 at the source's N=60.

children.text: Cosmic inflation
a.1. First Friedmann coefficient
For enclosed M=4πR³ρ/3, integrate R̈=−GM/R² to Ṙ²/2−GM/R=constant. Divide by R² and absorb the integration constant into curvature. This yields \(A_1=8\pi G/3\).
a.2. Adiabatic continuity
For E=ρVc² and V∝a³, dE=−pdV gives \(\dot\rho+3H(\rho+p/c^2)=0\). Therefore A2=3.
a.3. Equations of state

The continuity equation gives ρ∝a⁻³⁽¹⁺ʷ⁾. Radiation dilutes in number as a⁻³ and photon energy as a⁻¹, giving w=1/3. Nonrelativistic rest energy dilutes as a⁻³, giving w=0. Constant energy density has w=−1 and negative pressure.
a.4. Flat-universe scale factors

Radiation has \(a=(2H_0t)^{1/2}\). Matter has \(a=(3H_0t/2)^{2/3}\). Constant density has \(a=e^{H_0(t-t_0)}\). In the first two cases the time origin is the Big Bang and H0 refers to the epoch with a=1.
a.5. Curvature-density relation
Rearranging the first Friedmann equation gives \(k=(\Omega-1)H^2a^2R_s^2/c^2\). The source alternates Rs and R0 for the fixed reference radius.
a.6. Geometry ranges
For positive density, k=+1 corresponds to Ω>1, k=0 to Ω=1, and k=−1 to 0<Ω<1.
b.1. Flatness problem

The exact curvature relation is Ω−1=kc²/(Rs²a²H²). In a nearly flat era with a∝tᵖ and H=p/t this scales as t²⁻²ᵖ. It grows as t in radiation domination and t²ᐟ³ in matter domination. The expansion laws are the nearly flat approximation used in this argument.
b.2. Inflationary flattening
H is approximately constant and a∝exp(Ht), so \(\Omega(t)-1=[\Omega(t_i)-1]e^{-2H(t-t_i)}\). Curvature deviations decay exponentially.
b.3. Equivalent inflation conditions

Constant density implies p=−ρc². Differentiating Friedmann and using continuity gives \(\ddot a/a=-4\pi G(\rho+3p/c^2)/3\), hence positive acceleration. Since aH=ȧ, \(d[(aH)^{-1}]/dt=-\ddot a/\dot a^2<0\).
b.4. Slow-roll inflation bound
\(d[(aH)^{-1}]/dt=-(1+\dot H/H^2)/a=-(1-\epsilon)/a\). With a>0 this is negative exactly when ε<1.
c.1. Potential slow-roll formulas

From \(\dot H=-\dot\phi^2/(2M_{pl}^2)\), H²≈V/(3Mpl²) and 3Hφ̇≈−V′, obtain \[\epsilon\simeq\frac{M_{pl}^2}{2}\left(\frac{V^{\prime}}V\right)^2,\quad\eta_V\simeq M_{pl}^2\frac{V^{\prime\prime}}V,\quad\frac{dN}{d\phi}\simeq-\frac{V}{M_{pl}^2V^{\prime}}.\] These expressions require a monotonic field and the stated slow-roll approximation.
d.1. End of monomial inflation
\(\epsilon=n^2M_{pl}^2/(2\phi^2)\), giving \(\phi_{end}=|n|M_{pl}/\sqrt2\). The usual positive-n rolling branch has n>0. The n=0 constant potential never reaches ε=1 by this mechanism.
d.2. Observable constraints and e-fold sign

Integrating dN/dφ gives \(\phi^2=M_{pl}^2(n^2/2-2nN)\). Therefore \[r=\frac{16n}{n-4N},\qquad n_s=1-\frac{2(n+2)}{n-4N}.\] With the literal N=+60 used by the source, ns=0.968 gives n≈−5.93, but n=−6 gives r≈0.390>0.12. No integer fits both constraints. This positive N conflicts with dN=Hdt and N=0 at the end for a pre-end epoch. If 60 means remaining e-folds, use N=−60 here, or replace denominators by n+240. Then n=1 gives r≈0.0664, ns≈0.9751, just outside the stated tilt interval, and n=2 gives r≈0.132>0.12. Again no positive integer satisfies both. The sign issue is kept explicit and this comparison uses self-review.
